svg.title: More clerks, more orders?
svg.desc: Orders per minute rose 1.9–2.7× from 1 to 4 clerks, then levelled off or fell back: more clerks did not raise it by another 10% on any database (127–162 per minute with 8 and 16 clerks). Each extra clerk mostly added waiting: 95% of orders were saved within 1.54–2.29 s with 4 clerks and 9.32–12.8 s with 16. Different products, orders per minute, SQL Server: 1 clerk 81.2, 4 clerks 215, 8 clerks 147, 16 clerks 142. Different products, orders per minute, MySQL: 1 clerk 68.1, 4 clerks 130, 8 clerks 140, 16 clerks 133. Different products, orders per minute, PostgreSQL: 1 clerk 70.6, 4 clerks 158, 8 clerks 154, 16 clerks 148. Everyone sells the best-seller, orders per minute, SQL Server: 4 clerks 161, 8 clerks 162, 16 clerks 138. Everyone sells the best-seller, orders per minute, MySQL: 4 clerks 142, 8 clerks 127, 16 clerks 147. Everyone sells the best-seller, orders per minute, PostgreSQL: 4 clerks 156, 8 clerks 152, 16 clerks 155. Different products, 1 clerk verdict (judged on time per order): SQL Server fastest; MySQL 20% slower +145 ms vs SQL Server; PostgreSQL 15% slower +108 ms vs SQL Server. Different products, 4 clerks verdict: tie SQL Server’s runs varied 140–275/min. Everyone sells the best-seller, 4 clerks verdict: tie MySQL’s gap is within run-to-run swings. Different products, 8 clerks verdict: PostgreSQL joint fastest; SQL Server joint fastest ties with both; MySQL 10% slower vs PostgreSQL only. Everyone sells the best-seller, 8 clerks verdict: tie SQL Server’s runs varied 137–213/min. Different products, 16 clerks verdict: tie MySQL’s gap is within run-to-run swings. Everyone sells the best-seller, 16 clerks verdict: tie SQL Server’s gap is within run-to-run swings. Different products, 95% wait in seconds, SQL Server: 1 clerk 0.904, 4 clerks 1.54, 8 clerks 5.16, 16 clerks 10.9. Different products, 95% wait in seconds, MySQL: 1 clerk 1.01, 4 clerks 2.29, 8 clerks 4.75, 16 clerks 12.8. Different products, 95% wait in seconds, PostgreSQL: 1 clerk 0.962, 4 clerks 1.85, 8 clerks 4.37, 16 clerks 11.9. Everyone sells the best-seller, 95% wait in seconds, SQL Server: 4 clerks 1.86, 8 clerks 4.7, 16 clerks 11.5. Everyone sells the best-seller, 95% wait in seconds, MySQL: 4 clerks 2.21, 8 clerks 4.84, 16 clerks 12.2. Everyone sells the best-seller, 95% wait in seconds, PostgreSQL: 4 clerks 2.02, 8 clerks 4.43, 16 clerks 9.32.

g.font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', 'Helvetica Neue', Helvetica, Arial, 'Liberation Sans', sans-serif
g.text: Orders per minute rose 1.9–2.7× from 1 to 4 clerks, then levelled off or fell back: more clerks did not raise it
by another 10% on any database (127–162 per minute with 8 and 16 clerks). Each extra clerk mostly added
waiting: 95% of orders were saved within 1.54–2.29 s with 4 clerks and 9.32–12.8 s with 16.
Acumatica 2026 R2 · median of 6 runs per database and number of clerks · clerks work non-stop, with no pause between orders · Acumatica
ran on about 2 processor cores on every database
Line colour only tells the databases apart; it is not a verdict. The rows under each orders chart say whether users would notice the gap at that
Orders per minute, whole team – higher is better
each clerk’s orders are for different products
